knowledge_map.role: The rate at which a quantity changes.
Equations relating quantities and derivatives.
An equation together with a value at a starting point.
Different equation structures support different tools.
Conditions under which solutions exist and are unique.
Rearranges a separable equation so each variable can be integrated.
Transforms a first-order linear equation into a product derivative.
The rate depends on the state rather than explicitly on time.
Identify steady states and nearby behavior.
Several coupled first-order equations in matrix form.
Identify directions and rates for matrix systems.
May require generalized eigenvectors when there are too few eigenvectors.
Represents solutions of constant-coefficient homogeneous systems.
Depict trajectories and equilibrium behavior.
Evaluates the rate at a current state.
Uses a small step to approximate change.
Uses one slope per step.
Uses a predictor and averages two slopes.
Combines several estimated slopes per step.
One-step error starting from the exact state.
Total accumulated error at a target point.
Maps a time function to a function of a new variable.
A transform of a linear combination is the corresponding linear combination.
Turns a time derivative into an algebraic expression plus initial data.
Recovers a time function from a transform.

lecture_explainers.first_principles: If y(t) represents a quantity, its average rate of change over a short interval h is [y(t + h) − y(t)] / h. The derivative is the limit of that average as h approaches zero, when the limit exists.
lecture_explainers.derivation: For y(t) = t², [y(t + h) − y(t)] / h = [(t + h)² − t²] / h = 2t + h. As h approaches zero, the rate approaches 2t.
lecture_explainers.example: At t = 3, y′(3) = 6. Over a very short interval, the value initially increases at about 6 units per unit of time.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: From average change to instantaneous rate
graphic.caption: The derivative is the limit of the average rate as the interval becomes small.
steps: For y(t) = t²: the quotient simplifies to 2t + h
As h approaches 0, the derivative is 2t

lecture_explainers.first_principles: A differential equation \(y\prime=f(t,y)\) specifies the slope at each point. Starting from a known value, use that slope to estimate the value a small time step later.
lecture_explainers.derivation: For a short step \(h\), the definition of derivative suggests \[\frac{y(t+h)-y(t)}{h}\approx f(t,y(t)).\] Rearranging gives \(y(t+h)\approx y(t)+hf(t,y(t))\), an approximation in general.
lecture_explainers.example: If \(y\prime=t+y\) and \(y(0)=1\), one step of \(h=0.5\) gives \(y(0.5)\approx1+0.5(0+1)=1.5\).
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: One Euler step
graphic.caption: Use the current slope to estimate the next point.
steps: Start at the known point (t, y)
Move right by h and change y by approximately h × slope

lecture_explainers.first_principles: A separable equation has the form \(y\prime=g(t)h(y)\); its factors can be treated separately where \(h(y)\ne0\).
lecture_explainers.derivation: Since \(y\prime=dy/dt\), division and integration give \[\int\frac{dy}{h(y)}=\int g(t)\,dt+C\] on an interval where division is valid. Check excluded constant solutions separately.
lecture_explainers.example: For \(y\prime=2y\) and \(y(0)=1\), separation gives \(\ln|y|=2t+C\); the initial condition selects \(y=e^{2t}\).
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: Separation of variables
graphic.caption: An illustrative reasoning path.
steps: Identify the time and state factors
Separate where the state factor is nonzero
Integrate, use the initial value, and check excluded solutions

lecture_explainers.first_principles: A linear first-order equation has the form \(y\prime+p(t)y=q(t)\). An integrating factor makes its left side a product derivative.
lecture_explainers.derivation: The product rule gives \((\mu y)\prime=\mu y\prime+\mu\prime y\). Matching \(\mu(y\prime+py)\) requires \(\mu\prime=p\mu\); one choice is \[\mu=\exp\left(\int p(t)\,dt\right).\]
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: Integrating factors
graphic.caption: An illustrative reasoning path.
steps: Choose μ so that μ′ = pμ
Integrate (μy)′ = μq and apply the initial condition

lecture_explainers.first_principles: Improved Euler estimates the slope at both the beginning and a predicted end point, then averages them.
lecture_explainers.derivation: Let \(k_1=f(t_n,y_n)\), predict \(y^*=y_n+hk_1\), and take \(k_2=f(t_n+h,y^*)\). Averaging slopes gives \[y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac{h}{2}(k_1+k_2).\]
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: Improved Euler method
graphic.caption: An illustrative reasoning path.
steps: Predict the next value using Euler’s method
Calculate k₂ at the prediction and average the slopes

lecture_explainers.first_principles: A four-stage Runge–Kutta method combines several slope estimates across a step.
lecture_explainers.derivation: The classical method uses slopes \(k_1,k_2,k_3,k_4\) with weights \(1,2,2,1\): \[y_{n+1}=y_n+\frac{h}{6}(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4).\] Its error-order proof requires additional assumptions and a Taylor-series argument.
lecture_explainers.example: If \(y\prime=1\), every stage slope is \(1\), so the method advances \(y\) by exactly \(h\).
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.title: Runge–Kutta method
graphic.caption: An illustrative reasoning path.
steps: Estimate slopes at the start, midpoint and end
Advance the value by the weighted slope times h

lecture_explainers.first_principles: The Laplace transform expresses a function of time as an integral depending on \(s\), when that integral converges.
lecture_explainers.derivation: For \(f(t)=e^{at}\), the definition gives \[\int_0^\infty e^{-st}e^{at}\,dt=\frac{1}{s-a},\qquad s>a.\]
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

graphic.caption: An illustrative reasoning path.
steps: Integrate and state the convergence condition

categories.title: Estimating a solution with Euler’s method
categories.purpose: Identify the current point, calculate its slope, and take one or more numerical steps.

concepts.name: Slope at a point
concepts.explanation: For y′ = f(t, y), f(t, y) gives the instantaneous slope at that point.
concepts.derivation: The derivative is the limiting rate of change. Substituting the current t and y into f gives the local rate specified by the equation.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

concepts.name: Step size and approximation
concepts.explanation: The step size h is the change in t used for each estimate. The resulting estimate need not equal the exact solution.
concepts.derivation: Using slope × horizontal change to approximate vertical change gives y(next) ≈ y(current) + h × slope.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

example.problem: For \(y\prime=t+y\), \(y(0)=1\), estimate \(y(1)\) using two Euler steps of \(h=0.5\).
steps: After two steps \(t=1\), giving \(y(1)\approx2.5\); this is not the exact value.

progression.individual: First practise calculating f(t, y) at a given point and identifying a step size.
progression.combined: Then combine slope evaluation, repeated steps and an interpretation of numerical error.

graphic.title: A two-step Euler calculation
graphic.caption: Recalculate the slope after every step.

categories.title: Solve a first-order linear IVP
categories.purpose: Recognize a linear form and use the product rule.

concepts.name: Integrating factors
concepts.explanation: An integrating factor converts the linear left-hand side to a product derivative.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

steps: Use \(y(0)=1\) to obtain \(y=e^{-t}\), and check by substitution.

progression.individual: First recognize a linear equation and apply the product rule.
progression.combined: Then combine the factor, integration and initial condition.

concepts.name: Improved Euler method
concepts.explanation: Use the average of the starting and predicted ending slopes.
concepts.derivation: The predictor uses k₁, and the correction averages k₁ and k₂.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

example.problem: For y′=t+y, y(0)=1 and h=0.5, compute one improved Euler step.
steps: k₁=1 and the Euler predictor is 1.5.

progression.combined: Then combine a predictor, a second slope and an error interpretation.

categories.title: Evaluate a Laplace transform
categories.purpose: Use the definition and check convergence.

concepts.name: Laplace transform
concepts.explanation: The transform is an improper integral whose convergence depends on s.
concepts.derivation: For e^(at), direct integration gives 1/(s−a) when s>a.
sources: Illustrative material for this demonstration; not a course lecture.

steps: Combine exponentials in the defining integral.

progression.individual: First practise exponent laws and improper integrals.
progression.combined: Then combine convergence, transform properties and an IVP.
